items: 1Differentiate between nucleosides and nucleotides — a nucleoside is base + sugar; a nucleotide adds a phosphate group.

blocks.x: Core definitions
Nucleotide A phosphate ester of a pentose sugar in which a nitrogenous base is covalently linked to C1' of the sugar; the monomeric unit of nucleic acids.
Nucleoside A base + sugar compound lacking the phosphate group. A 5'-nucleotide may be called nucleoside-5'-phosphate.
Nucleic acid A linear polymer of nucleotides whose phosphate groups bridge the 3' and 5' positions of successive sugar residues; at physiological pH, nucleic acids are polyanions.
Base + Sugar→ Nucleoside→ + Phosphate→ Nucleotide→ Polynucleotide→ DNA / RNA
Biologically ubiquitous roles
Nucleotides and their derivatives participate in nearly all biochemical processes:

items: They form the monomeric units of nucleic acids, storing and expressing genetic information.
Nucleoside triphosphates, most obviously ATP, are the energy-rich end products of energy-releasing pathways.
Most metabolic pathways are regulated, at least in part, by nucleotide levels such as ATP and ADP.
Nucleotide derivatives such as NAD, FAD and coenzyme A are required members in many enzymatic reactions.
As components of enzyme-like nucleic acids called ribozymes, nucleotides have catalytic activities themselves.

blocks.x: Building blocks
Nucleotides are phosphate esters of a pentose sugar with a nitrogenous base attached at C1' — the fundamental monomer of every nucleic acid.
Sugar, base and phosphate
Ribonucleotides
RNA monomeric units. The pentose sugar is D-ribose.
Deoxyribonucleotides
DNA monomeric units (deoxynucleotides). The pentose sugar is 2'-deoxy-D-ribose.

The phosphate group may be bonded to C5' of the pentose to form a 5'-nucleotide or to C3' to form a 3'-nucleotide. If the phosphate group is absent, the compound is a nucleoside. Note: nucleotide phosphate groups are doubly ionised at physiological pH — nucleotides are moderately strong acids.
Purines & pyrimidines
Purines — 6+5 membered rings

Adenine and guanine: a heterocyclic aromatic compound with a pyrimidine ring fused to an imidazole ring. Purines form glycosidic bonds to ribose via their N9 atoms. Electron-deficient (reactive) positions: 2, 6 and 8.
Pyrimidines — 6-membered ring

Cytosine, uracil (mainly RNA) and thymine (5-methyluracil, mainly DNA): a pyrimidine ring with nitrogens at positions 1 and 3. Pyrimidines bond via their N1 atoms. Electron-deficient positions: 2, 4 and 6 — position 6 is most reactive toward additions, position 2 least.
Base → nucleoside → nucleotide
UV absorption of nucleic acids

items: Nucleic acids strongly absorb UV light below 300 nm, with an absorption max at ~260 nm and a stronger one below 200 nm.
Biologically significant because it induces mutations, a natural result of exposure to sunlight.
In the lab, this property helps identify and quantitatively analyse nucleotides.
The A260/A280 ratio assesses purity: pure DNA ≈1.8, pure RNA ≈2.0.

blocks.x: Charge, ionisation & reactivity of bases

items: The ionised phosphate groups of the polymer backbone give nucleic acid molecules a high negative charge.
DNA is usually associated with proteins such as histones or protamines (in spermatozoa), with polycations such as spermidine or alkaline earth cations such as Mg²⁺.
If the pH of a double helical DNA solution is lowered to ~3 or raised to ~12, the two strands unwind and can be separated.
Over the entire pH range, the alternating sugar-phosphate backbone remains negatively charged.
Purines and pyrimidines are relatively stable, aromatic compounds, but react with many reagents and can be fully degraded under mild conditions.
Reaction rates are influenced by position in the polynucleotide chain and whether the nucleic acid is single- or double-stranded.
Most reactions are nucleophilic addition or displacement reactions at electron-deficient ring positions.
Reactions of nucleic acids are essentially the same as those of individual nucleosides or nucleotides.

blocks.x: Molecular architecture
Elucidated primarily in the early 1950s: nucleic acids are directional polymers held together by base pairing, and organised across four structural levels.
The phosphodiester backbone

Nucleic acids are linear polymers of nucleotides whose phosphate groups bridge the 3' and 5' positions of successive sugar residues via phosphodiester bonds. Polynucleotides have directionality: each has a 5' end (C5' not linked to a neighbouring nucleotide) and a 3' end (C3' not attached to an adjacent nucleotide). Sequences are conventionally written 5'→3', e.g. 5' C-A-G 3'.
Base composition of DNA

items: DNA has equal numbers of adenine and thymine residues (A = T) and equal numbers of guanine and cytosine residues (G = C).
The base composition of DNA from a given organism is characteristic of that organism, independent of tissue, age, nutritional state or other environmental factors.
Base composition varies among organisms — 25% to 75% G=C in different bacterial species — but is constant among related species; in mammals, G=C ranges 39%–46%.

Single-stranded RNA has no apparent constraint on base composition, but double-stranded RNA (genetic material of certain viruses) also obeys Chargaff's rules, with A pairing with U as it does with T in DNA.
A—T pairs form 2 hydrogen bonds; G—C pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds — the DNA double helix has a major and a minor groove.

The strength of hydrogen bonding between bases is roughly equal to the enthalpy of the base-pairing reaction; strong interaction with polar solvents via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic effects makes exact bond strength hard to measure.
The small energies summed over the many base pairs in a DNA molecule help stabilise the overall structure.
Some DNAs contain chemical derivatives of the standard bases; dA and dC in many organisms are partially replaced by N6-methyl-dA and 5-methyl-dC.
Sequence-specific enzymatic modification generates the altered bases. Modified DNAs still obey Chargaff's rules if derivatised bases are taken as equivalent to their parent bases.
Many bases in RNA, especially transfer RNAs (tRNAs), are derivatised.

blocks.title: Why DNA (not RNA) is the genetic archive

blocks.x: RNA is highly susceptible to base-catalysed hydrolysis, yielding a mixture of 2' and 3' nucleotides, because its ribose carries a 2'-OH group. DNA, which lacks the 2'-OH group, is resistant to base-catalysed hydrolysis and is much more chemically stable than RNA — probably why DNA evolved to be the cellular genetic archive.
From single chain to chromatin

1PrimaryA single DNA chain: the backbone where deoxyribose units are linked by covalent phosphodiester bridges between 3' and 5' hydroxyls of adjacent sugars. 2SecondarySteric relationship of nearby bases — the double helical structure. Bases lie at the centre; sugar-phosphate backbone is on the outside. Includes helix, stem-loop and pseudoknot forms. 3TertiaryAtoms' locations in 3D space with geometric/steric constraints — DNA can be relaxed, looped or superhelical. Includes A-DNA, B-DNA and Z-DNA forms. 4QuaternaryHigher-level organisation: interactions of nucleic acids with other molecules, e.g. chromatin with histones, or separate RNA units in the ribosome/spliceosome.
Packaging path: DNA double helix → wraps histone proteins → nucleosomes → coiled chromatin → condensed chromosome.
Melting, hyperchromicity & Tm

items: Heating a duplex DNA solution above a characteristic temperature causes its native structure to collapse (denature): the two complementary strands separate into a flexible, fluctuating random coil.
The characteristic high viscosity of DNA solutions (from resistance to deformation of rigid, rod-like duplex molecules) hugely declines on denaturation to two freely-jointed single strands.
When DNA denatures, its UV absorbance increases by ~40% at all wavelengths — the hyperchromic effect, from disrupted electronic interactions among nearby bases (monitored at 260 nm).

Collapse of part of the duplex destabilises the remainder — a cooperative process. Denaturation is described as the melting of a one-dimensional solid, with a melting curve; the midpoint temperature is the melting temperature, Tm.

Tm depends on solvent, ion identity/concentration and pH. Duplex DNA denatures (Tm decreases) under alkaline conditions. Tm increases linearly with the mole fraction of G–C base pairs, since triple hydrogen-bonded G–C pairs are more stable than double hydrogen-bonded A–T pairs.

blocks.x: DNA as the repository of information

items: DNA is a large molecule with infinite variety, so it can store enormous amounts of information.
It is the repository of all information the cell requires; most information directs protein synthesis. Genes encode the information that determines a protein's primary structure.
The structure of proteins dictates protein activity, which determines the physiological role of the cell.
DNA undergoes faithful replication, ensuring information is transmitted through generations, and is a stable molecule resisting hydrolysis and mutation.

blocks.x: Gene expression machinery

RNA is a family of large biomolecules performing crucial roles in the regulation and expression of genes. With DNA, RNA comprises the nucleic acids, which with proteins are the three major macromolecules essential for life.
How RNA differs from DNA

items: RNA is usually a single-stranded molecule with a much shorter chain of nucleotides, though complementary base pairing can form intra-strand double helices, as in tRNA.
RNA contains ribose (with a 2'-OH group DNA lacks). These hydroxyl groups make RNA less stable than DNA — RNA is more prone to hydrolysis.
The complementary base to adenine in RNA is not thymine but uracil, an unmethylated form of thymine.

blocks.x: Most RNAs (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and other ncRNAs) have self-complementary sequences allowing them to fold into short helices packed together like proteins, rather than one long double helix. RNAs can also achieve chemical catalysis like enzymes — e.g. the ribosome's peptide-bond-forming active site is composed entirely of RNA.
Types of RNA and their functions

Conveys genetic information from DNA to the ribosome, specifying the amino acid sequence of proteins. After transcription as pre-mRNA (processed by RNA polymerase) and processing, mature mRNA is translated. Information is encoded as codons of three bases each.

Mediates codon recognition, providing the matching amino acid. Archaically called sRNA (soluble RNA); typically 73–94 nucleotides, an adaptor linking nucleotide sequence to amino acid sequence via its anticodon.

The RNA component of the ribosome, ~60% rRNA and 40% protein by weight. Ribosomes contain two major rRNAs (LSU & SSU) plus 50+ proteins. The LSU rRNA acts as a ribozyme, catalysing peptide bond formation. rRNA sequences are used to trace evolutionary relationships, being of ancient origin.

Also called U-RNA; small RNAs (~150 nucleotides) found in eukaryotic nuclei, transcribed by RNA polymerase II or III. Their primary function is processing pre-mRNA (heterogeneous nuclear RNA, hnRNA) in the nucleus.

items: A functional RNA molecule not translated into a protein. Synonyms: non-protein-coding RNA (npcRNA), non-messenger RNA (nmRNA), functional RNA (fRNA); short bacterial ncRNAs are often called sRNA.
The DNA sequence from which a non-coding RNA is transcribed is called an RNA gene.
ncRNA genes include highly abundant, functionally essential RNAs such as tRNA and rRNA, as well as noRNAs, miRNAs, siRNAs, snRNAs, exRNAs, piRNAs and lncRNAs.

blocks.x: Role of RNA in protein synthesis
DNA→ Transcription→ pre-mRNA (hnRNA)→ snRNA processing→ Mature mRNA→ Ribosome (rRNA)→ tRNA delivers a.a.→ Protein
At the ribosome, tRNAs occupy the A and P sites, matching codons on mRNA to build the growing polypeptide, while rRNA forms the catalytic core of the large subunit.
Clinical biochemistry
Purine and pyrimidine breakdown products, and synthetic analogues that mimic them, have important roles in both disease and drug therapy.
Hypoxanthine, xanthine & uric acid
Deamination products catabolism
When adenine is deaminated, hypoxanthine is formed; deamination of guanine gives xanthine. Both are enzymatically oxidised to give uric acid.
Gout disease
Uric acid can form sodium salts that deposit in soft tissues, giving rise to inflammation of affected tissues — the condition known as gout.
Nucleic acid analogues as drugs

Nucleic acid analogues are compounds with structures like purines and pyrimidines (or their nucleosides) that can be exploited as drugs, including anticancer or antimicrobial agents. Examples include 5-fluorouracil and zidovudine.
Other nucleic acid analogues have pharmacological activities, such as caffeine, theobromine and theophylline — naturally occurring purine derivatives with stimulant/bronchodilator effects.
Nucleoside analogue drugs
Because these analogues resemble the natural bases/nucleosides, they can be incorporated into, or interfere with, nucleic acid metabolism in target cells — the basis of their therapeutic action.
